danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Fyrst Vasilij var ikke en mand, der bevidst gennemtænkte sine planer. Endnu mindre tænkte han på at skade nogen til sin egen fordel. Han var blot en verdensmand, der havde gjort karriere, og for hvem det at gøre karriere var blevet en vane. Planer og udspil, som han aldrig rigtig gjorde sig rede for, men som udgjorde hele hans livs interesse, tog ustandselig form i hans hoved, fremkaldt af de omstændigheder og mennesker, han mødte. Af sådanne planer havde han ikke blot én eller to i hovedet, men dusinvis — nogle kun i svøb, andre ved at nå deres mål, og atter andre i færd med at gå i opløsning. Han sagde for eksempel ikke til sig selv: »Den mand har indflydelse, jeg må vinde hans tillid og venskab og gennem ham opnå en særlig bevilling.« Ej heller sagde han til sig selv: »Pierre er en rig mand, jeg må lokke ham til at gifte sig med min datter og låne mig de fyrre tusind rubler, jeg har brug for.« Men når han stødte på en mand af indflydelse, fortalte hans instinkt ham straks, at denne mand kunne være nyttig, og uden forudberegning greb fyrst Vasilij den første lejlighed til at vinde hans tillid, smigre ham, blive fortrolig med ham og endelig fremsætte sin anmodning.

Han havde Pierre ved hånden i Moskva og skaffede ham en udnævnelse som kammerherre, der på den tid medførte rang af statsråd, og insisterede på, at den unge mand skulle ledsage ham til Sankt Petersborg og bo i hans hus. Med tilsyneladende åndsfraværelse, men dog med den urokkelige sikkerhed, at han handlede rigtigt, gjorde fyrst Vasilij alt for at få Pierre gift med sin datter. Havde han tænkt sine planer igennem på forhånd, kunne han ikke have været så naturlig og vist en sådan ukunstlet fortrolighed i omgangen med alle, både over og under sig i den sociale rangorden. Noget drog ham altid mod de rigere og mægtigere, og han besad en sjælden evne til at gribe det mest gunstige øjeblik til at benytte sig af folk.

Pierre, der uventet var blevet greve Bezukhov og rigmand, følte sig efter sin nylige ensomhed og frihed fra bekymringer så omringet og optaget, at det kun var i sengen, han kunne være alene. Han måtte underskrive papirer, give møde på offentlige kontorer, hvis formål var ham uklar, udspørge sin forvalter, besøge sit gods nær Moskva og modtage mange mennesker, der tidligere ikke engang havde ønsket at vide af hans eksistens, men som nu ville have været fornærmede og bedrøvede, om han havde valgt ikke at se dem. Disse forskellige mennesker — forretningsmænd, slægtninge og bekendte — var alle tilbøjelige til at behandle den unge arving med den største venlighed og smiger: de var alle tydeligvis fast overbevist om Pierres ædle egenskaber. Han hørte stadig sådanne vendinger som: »Med Deres bemærkelsesværdige godhed,« eller: »Med Deres fortræffelige hjerte,« »De er selv så hæderlig, greve,« eller: »Var han bare så klog som Dem,« og så videre, indtil han oprigtigt begyndte at tro på sin egen enestående godhed og overordentlige intelligens, så meget desto mere som det i hans hjertes dyb altid havde forekommet ham, at han virkelig var meget god og intelligent. Selv folk, der tidligere havde været ondskabsfulde over for ham og åbenlyst uvenlige, blev nu milde og kærlige. Den ældste, vrede prinsesse med det lange liv og det plaskredes hår var kommet ind i Pierres værelse efter begravelsen. Med sænkede øjne og hyppige rødmen fortalte hun ham, at hun var meget ked af deres tidligere misforståelser og ikke følte, at hun nu havde ret til at bede ham om noget — kun om tilladelse, efter det slag hun havde modtaget, til at forblive nogle uger endnu i det hus, hun elskede så højt, og hvor hun havde ofret så meget. Hun kunne ikke holde tårerne tilbage. Rørt over at denne statueagtige prinsesse kunne forandre sig sådan, tog Pierre hendes hånd og bad om hendes tilgivelse, uden at vide for hvad. Fra den dag forandrede den ældste prinsesse sig fuldstændigt over for Pierre og begyndte at strikke et stribet tørklæde til ham.
»Gør dette for min skyld, mon cher; hun har trods alt måttet finde sig i meget fra den afdøde,« sagde fyrst Vasilij til ham og rakte ham et dokument til underskrift til prinsessens fordel.

Fyrst Vasilij var nået til den slutning, at det var nødvendigt at kaste dette ben — en veksel på tredive tusind rubler — til den stakkels prinsesse, for at det ikke skulle falde hende ind at tale om hans andel i sagen med den indlagte portefølje. Pierre underskrev dokumentet, og derefter blev prinsessen endnu venligere. De yngre søstre blev også kærlige mod ham, især den yngste, den smukke med skønhedspletten, der ofte bragte ham i forlegenhed med sine smil og sin egen forvirring, når hun mødte ham.

Det forekom Pierre så naturligt, at alle skulle kunne lide ham, og det ville have forekommet ham så unaturligt, om nogen ikke kunne, at han ikke kunne andet end at tro på oprigtigheden hos dem omkring ham. Desuden havde han ingen tid til at spørge sig selv, om disse mennesker var oprigtige eller ej. Han var altid travlt optaget og følte sig i en tilstand af mild og munter beruselse. Han følte sig som midtpunkt for en vigtig, almén bevægelse; at man stadig ventede noget af ham; at hvis han ikke gjorde det, ville han skuffe og bedrøve mange, men at hvis han gjorde det og det, ville alt gå godt; og han gjorde, hvad der blev forlangt af ham, men det lykkelige resultat lå stadig i fremtiden.

Mere end nogen anden tog fyrst Vasilij Pierre i besiddelse — hans affærer og ham selv — i de første dage. Fra grev Bezukhovs død slap han ikke den unge mand. Han optrådte som en mand, der var tynget af forretninger, træt og lidende, men som dog ikke for medlidenhedens skyld ville overlade denne hjælpeløse unge mand — der trods alt var hans gamle vens søn og besidder af en uhyre formue — til skæbnens luner og slynglernes rænker. I de få dage han tilbragte i Moskva efter grev Bezukhovs død, kaldte han Pierre til sig, eller gik selv til ham, og fortalte ham, hvad der burde gøres, i en tone af træthed og selvsikkerhed, som om han hver gang tilføjede: »Du ved, at jeg er overvældet af forretninger, og det er rent ud af barmhjertighed, at jeg plager mig med dig, og du ved også godt, at det, jeg foreslår, er det eneste mulige.«

»Nå, min kære, i morgen rejser vi endelig,« sagde fyrst Vasilij en dag, idet han lukkede øjnene og klappede Pierre på albuen — han talte, som om han sagde noget, der for længst var aftalt og ikke længere kunne ændres. »Vi rejser i morgen, og jeg giver dig en plads i min karet. Jeg er meget glad. Alle vores vigtige forretninger her er nu i orden, og jeg burde være rejst for længst. Her er noget, jeg har modtaget fra kansleren. Jeg bad ham om det for din skyld, og du er optaget i diplomatiet og udnævnt til kammerherre. Den diplomatiske karriere ligger nu åben for dig.«

Trods den tone af træt selvfølgelighed, hvormed disse ord blev sagt, ønskede Pierre, der så længe havde overvejet sin karriere, at komme med et forslag. Men fyrst Vasilij afbrød ham i den særlige dybe, kurrende tone, der udelukkede enhver mulighed for at bryde ind, og som han brugte i yderste tilfælde, når særlig overtalelse var nødvendig.

»Mais, mon cher, jeg gjorde det for min egen skyld, for at berolige min samvittighed, og du behøver ikke at takke mig. Ingen har endnu klaget over at blive elsket for meget; og desuden er du fri — du kan give det op i morgen. Men du vil selv se alt, når du kommer til Petersborg. Det er på høje tid for dig at komme bort fra alle de forfærdelige minder.« Fyrst Vasilij sukkede. »Ja, ja, min dreng. Og min kammertjener kan køre i din karet. Ah! Jeg havde nær glemt,« tilføjede han. »Du ved, mon cher, din far og jeg havde nogle mellemregnskaber, så jeg har modtaget, hvad der tilkom mig fra Rjazan-godset, og beholder det; du får ikke brug for det. Vi gennemgår regnskaberne senere.«
Med »hvad der tilkom fra Rjazan-godset« mente fyrst Vasilij adskillige tusind rubler i landskyld, som han havde inddrevet fra Pierres bønder og beholdt for sig selv.

I Petersborg, ligesom i Moskva, fandt Pierre den samme atmosfære af venlighed og hengivenhed. Han kunne ikke afslå den post — eller rettere den rang (for han foretog sig intet) — som fyrst Vasilij havde skaffet ham, og bekendtskaber, invitationer og selskabelige forpligtelser var så talrige, at han endnu mere end i Moskva følte en fornemmelse af forvirring, travlhed og en stadig forventning om noget godt, der altid lå foran ham, men aldrig blev nået.

Af hans tidligere ungkarlebekendtskaber var mange ikke længere i Petersborg. Garden var draget i felten; Dolokhov var degraderet til menig; Anatole var et sted i provinserne med hæren; fyrst Andrej var i udlandet — og så havde Pierre ikke mulighed for at tilbringe sine aftener, som han plejede, eller åbne sit hjerte i en fortrolig samtale med en ældre ven, han respekterede. Hele hans tid gik med middage og baller og blev hovedsagelig tilbragt i fyrst Vasilijs hus i selskab med den svære prinsesse, hans hustru, og hans smukke datter Hélène.
Ligesom de andre viste Anna Pavlovna Scherer Pierre den holdningsændring over for ham, der var sket i selskabet.

Tidligere havde Pierre i Anna Pavlovnas nærhed altid følt, at det, han sagde, var malplaceret, taktløst og upassende, at bemærkninger, der syntes ham kloge, mens de formede sig i hans tanker, blev dumme, så snart han udtalte dem, mens Hippolytes dummeste bemærkninger derimod blev kloge og velformulerede. Nu var alt, hvad Pierre sagde, charmant. Selv om Anna Pavlovna ikke sagde det, kunne han se, at hun gerne ville, men kun afstod af hensyn til hans beskedenhed.
I begyndelsen af vinteren 1805-06 modtog Pierre en af Anna Pavlovnas sædvanlige lyserøde indbydelser med tilføjelsen: »De vil møde den smukke Hélène her — hende, det altid er en fryd at se.«

Da han læste den sætning, følte Pierre for første gang, at der var vokset et bånd mellem ham og Hélène, som andre mennesker anerkendte, og den tanke alarmerede ham, som om en forpligtelse blev pålagt ham, som han ikke kunne opfylde, og behagede ham som en underholdende antagelse.

Anna Pavlovnas »at home« lignede det forrige, blot var den nyhed, hun tilbød sine gæster denne gang, ikke Mortemart, men en diplomat nyligt fra Berlin med de allersidste detaljer om kejser Alexanders besøg i Potsdam, og om hvordan de to ophøjede venner havde lovet hinanden i en ubrydelig alliance at forsvare retfærdighedens sag mod menneskehedens fjende. Anna Pavlovna modtog Pierre med et anstrøg af vemod, der åbenbart hentydte til den unge mands nylige tab ved grev Bezukhovs død (alle følte det som en pligt at forsikre Pierre, at han var dybt ramt af faderens død — en far, han næppe havde kendt), og hendes vemod lignede den ophøjede vemod, hun lagde for dagen ved omtalen af Hendes Majestæt kejserinde Marja Fjodorovna. Pierre følte sig smigret herover. Anna Pavlovna arrangerede de forskellige grupper i sin salon med sin sædvanlige dygtighed. Den store gruppe, hvori fyrst Vasilij og generalerne befandt sig, nød godt af diplomaten. En anden gruppe var ved tebordet. Pierre ville gerne slutte sig til den første, men Anna Pavlovna — der var i den ophidsede tilstand som en kommandør på slagmarken, hvem tusinde nye og strålende idéer falder ind, og som der knap er tid til at virkeliggøre — greb Pierres ærme med fingeren, idet hun fik øje på ham, og sagde:

»Vent lidt, jeg har noget i tankerne for Dem i aften.« (Hun kastede et blik på Hélène og smilede til hende.) »Min kære Hélène, vær barmhjertig mod min stakkels tante, som tilbeder Dem. Tag hen og hold hende med selskab i ti minutter. Og for at det ikke skal blive alt for kedeligt, her er den kære greve, som sikkert ikke nægter at ledsage Dem.«
Skønheden gik hen til tanten, men Anna Pavlovna holdt Pierre tilbage, som om hun havde et sidste nødvendigt ord at sige.

»Er hun ikke udsøgt?« sagde hun til Pierre og pegede på den statelige skønhed, der gled bort. »Og den holdning! For en så ung pige — en sådan takt, en sådan mesterlig fuldkommenhed i manerer! Det kommer fra hjertet. Lykkelig den mand, der vinder hende! Med hende ville den mindst verdslige mand indtage den mest strålende position i selskabet. Synes De ikke? Jeg ønskede blot at høre Deres mening,« og Anna Pavlovna lod Pierre gå.

Pierre var i sit svar oprigtigt enig i hendes bedømmelse af Hélènes fuldkomne manerer. Hvis han nogensinde tænkte på Hélène, var det netop på hendes skønhed og hendes bemærkelsesværdige evne til at virke tavst og værdig i selskabslivet.

Den gamle tante modtog de to unge i sit hjørne, men syntes snarere at ville skjule sin tilbedelse af Hélène og viste i stedet sin frygt for Anna Pavlovna. Hun kiggede på sin niece, som for at spørge, hvad hun skulle stille op med disse mennesker. Da Anna Pavlovna forlod dem, rørte hun atter Pierres ærme og sagde: »Jeg håber, De ikke igen vil sige, det er kedeligt i mit hus,« og hun så på Hélène.

Hélène smilede med et blik, der antydede, at hun ikke indrømmede muligheden af, at nogen kunne se hende uden at blive betaget. Tanten hostede, sank en klump og sagde på fransk, at hun var meget glad for at se Hélène — derpå henvendte hun sig til Pierre med de samme velkomstord og det samme blik. Midt i en kedelig og famlende samtale vendte Hélène sig mod Pierre med det smukt strålende smil, hun skænkede alle. Pierre var så vant til det smil, og det betød så lidt for ham, at han ikke lagde mærke til det. Tanten talte netop om en samling snustobaksdåser, der havde tilhørt Pierres far, grev Bezukhov, og viste dem sin egen dåse. Prinsesse Hélène bad om at se portrættet af tantens mand på dåsens låg.

»Det er sandsynligvis Vinesses værk,« sagde Pierre, idet han nævnte en berømt miniaturemaler, og han bøjede sig over bordet for at tage dåsen, mens han forsøgte at opfange, hvad der blev sagt ved det andet bord.

Han rejste sig halvt, da han ville gå rundt, men tanten rakte ham dåsen henover Hélènes ryg. Hélène bøjede sig frem for at give plads og kiggede rundt med et smil. Hun var, som altid til aftenselskaber, iført en kjole, der på den tid var moderne, skåret meget dybt foran og bagpå. Hendes barm, der altid havde virket som marmor for Pierre, var nu så tæt på ham, at hans nærsynede øjne ikke kunne undgå at opfatte den levende ynde i hendes hals og skuldre, så nær hans læber, at han blot behøvede at bøje hovedet en smule for at berøre dem. Han var bevidst om varmen fra hendes krop, duften af parfume og knirken fra hendes korset, når hun bevægede sig. Han så ikke hendes marmorne skønhed, der dannede et hele med hendes kjole, men hele ynden af hendes krop, kun dækket af hendes klæder. Og da han først havde set dette, kunne han ikke lade være med at være bevidst om det, ligesom vi ikke kan genoptage en illusion, vi har gennemskuet.

»Så De har aldrig før lagt mærke til, hvor smuk jeg er?« syntes Hélène at sige. »De havde ikke bemærket, at jeg er en kvinde? Ja, jeg er en kvinde, som kan tilhøre enhver — også Dem,« sagde hendes blik. Og i det øjeblik følte Pierre, at Hélène ikke blot kunne, men nødvendigvis måtte blive hans hustru, og at det ikke kunne være anderledes.

Han vidste det i det øjeblik lige så sikkert, som om han havde stået ved alteret med hende. Hvordan og hvornår det ville ske, vidste han ikke, han vidste ikke engang, om det ville være en god ting (han følte endda, han vidste ikke hvorfor, at det ville være en dårlig ting), men han vidste, at det ville ske.

Pierre slog øjnene ned, løftede dem igen og ønskede atter at se hende som en fjern skønhed, langt fra ham, som han havde set hende hver dag indtil da, men han kunne ikke længere. Han kunne det ikke, ligesom en mand, der har set en tot steppegræs gennem tågen og troet, det var et træ, ikke atter kan se det som et træ, når han først har genkendt det som græs. Hun var forfærdende tæt på ham. Hun havde allerede magt over ham, og mellem dem var der ikke længere nogen barriere end hans egen viljes barriere.
»Nå, jeg forlader Dem i Deres lille krog,« lød Anna Pavlovnas stemme. »Jeg kan se, De har det godt dér.«
Og Pierre, der nervøst forsøgte at erindre, om han havde gjort noget upassende, så sig om med et rødmende ansigt. Det syntes ham, at alle vidste, hvad der var hændt ham, ligesom han selv vidste det.
Lidt senere, da han gik hen til den store kreds, sagde Anna Pavlovna til ham: »Jeg hører, De lader Deres Petersborg-hus sætte i stand?«
Det var sandt. Arkitekten havde sagt, det var nødvendigt, og Pierre, uden at vide hvorfor, lod sit enorme Petersborg-hus istandsætte.

»Det er godt, men flyt ikke fra fyrst Vasilij. Det er godt at have en ven som fyrsten,« sagde hun med et smil til fyrst Vasilij. »Jeg ved noget om det, gør jeg ikke? Og De er stadig så ung. De har brug for råd. Bliv ikke vred over, at en gammel kvinde tager sig den frihed.«

Hun holdt en pause, som kvinder altid gør, når de har nævnt deres alder. »Hvis De gifter Dem, bliver det en anden sag,« fortsatte hun og forenede dem begge i ét blik. Pierre så ikke på Hélène, og hun ikke på ham. Men hun var lige så forfærdende tæt på ham. Han mumlede noget og blev rød.

Da han kom hjem, kunne han ikke falde i søvn i lang tid for at tænke over, hvad der var sket. Hvad var der sket? Intet. Han havde blot forstået, at den kvinde, han havde kendt som barn, og om hvis skønhed han fraværende havde sagt: »Ja, hun er smuk,« — han havde forstået, at denne kvinde kunne tilhøre ham.

»Men hun er dum. Jeg har selv sagt, hun er dum,« tænkte han. »Der er noget modbydigt, noget forkert, i den følelse, hun vækker i mig. Man har fortalt mig, at hendes bror Anatole var forelsket i hende og hun i ham, at der var en hel skandale, og at det er derfor, han blev sendt bort. Hippolyte er hendes bror... fyrst Vasilij er hendes far... Det er forkert...« tænkte han, men mens han tænkte dette (tanken var endnu ufuldstændig), opdagede han, at han smilede, og blev bevidst om, at en anden tankerække var sprunget frem, og mens han tænkte på hendes værdiløshed, drømte han også om, hvordan hun ville blive hans hustru, hvordan hun ville elske ham og blive helt anderledes, og at alt, hvad han havde tænkt og hørt om hende, måske var usandt. Og han så hende igen for sig — ikke som fyrst Vasilijs datter, men forestillede sig hele hendes krop, kun sløret af den grå kjole. »Men nej! Hvorfor er den tanke aldrig faldet mig ind før?« og atter sagde han til sig selv, at det var umuligt, at der ville være noget unaturligt og, som det syntes ham, vanærende i dette ægteskab. Han mindedes hendes tidligere ord og blikke og ordene og blikkene fra dem, der havde set dem sammen. Han huskede Anna Pavlovnas ord og blikke, da hun talte til ham om hans hus, huskede tusindvis af lignende antydninger fra fyrst Vasilij og andre og blev grebet af rædsel ved tanken om, at han måske allerede på en eller anden måde havde bundet sig til at gøre noget, der tydeligvis var forkert, og som han ikke burde gøre. Men i det selvsamme øjeblik, han udtrykte denne overbevisning for sig selv, rejste hendes billede sig i en anden del af hans bevidsthed i al sin kvindelige skønhed.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Prince Vasili was not a man who carefully planned things out. Even less did he deliberately scheme to hurt anyone for his own benefit. He was simply a man of the world who had learned how to get ahead, and getting ahead had become second nature to him. Plans and strategies that he never quite acknowledged to himself, but that made up the entire interest of his life, were constantly forming in his mind, sparked by the people and situations he encountered. He didn't have just one or two such plans going at once, but dozens—some barely taking shape, some nearing completion, and some already falling apart. He never said to himself, for instance, 'This man has influence, so I need to win his trust and use him to get a special appointment.' Nor did he think, 'Pierre is rich, so I should get him to marry my daughter and lend me forty thousand rubles.' But whenever he met someone powerful, his instincts immediately told him that person could be useful, and without any forethought, Prince Vasili would seize the first opportunity to gain his confidence, flatter him, become close to him, and eventually make his request.

He had Pierre right there in Moscow, so he arranged an appointment for him as Gentleman of the Bedchamber—which at the time carried the status of Councilor of State—and insisted the young man come with him to Petersburg and stay at his house. With what looked like absent-mindedness, yet with unwavering confidence that he was doing the right thing, Prince Vasili did everything to get Pierre to marry his daughter. If he had actually planned it all out, he couldn't have been so natural or shown such relaxed familiarity with people both above and below him in social standing. Something always drew him toward those richer and more powerful than himself, and he had a rare talent for choosing exactly the right moment to use people.

Pierre, who had unexpectedly become Count Bezukhov and a rich man, felt so overwhelmed after his recent loneliness and freedom that he could only be by himself in bed. He had to sign papers, visit government offices whose purpose he didn't understand, consult his head steward, inspect his estate near Moscow, and receive a stream of people who had previously ignored his existence but would now have been offended if he hadn't seen them. All of these people—businessmen, relatives, acquaintances—treated the young heir with the greatest friendliness and flattery. They were all obviously convinced of Pierre's fine qualities. He kept hearing things like: 'With your remarkable kindness,' or 'With your excellent heart,' 'You are such an honorable man, Count,' or 'If only he were as clever as you.' He began to genuinely believe in his own exceptional kindness and extraordinary intelligence, especially since, deep down, he had always felt he really was kind and intelligent. Even people who had been unfriendly before now became warm and affectionate. The stern eldest princess, with her long waist and doll-like plastered-down hair, had come to Pierre's room after the funeral. With lowered eyes and frequent blushes, she told him she was sorry about their past disagreements and now felt she had no right to ask anything—only permission, after the blow she had suffered, to stay a few more weeks in the house she loved so much and where she had sacrificed so much. She couldn't hold back her tears. Moved by this transformation in the stiff princess, Pierre took her hand and begged her forgiveness, without knowing what for. From that day on, the eldest princess completely changed toward Pierre and even began knitting him a striped scarf.
"Do this for me, my dear—after all, she had to put up with a great deal from the deceased," said Prince Vasili, handing Pierre a document to sign for the princess's benefit.

Prince Vasili had decided it was necessary to throw this bone—a thirty-thousand-ruble payment—to the poor princess, so it wouldn't occur to her to talk about his role in the affair of the inlaid portfolio. Pierre signed the document, and after that the princess became even kinder. The younger sisters also grew affectionate toward him, especially the youngest, the pretty one with the mole, who often made him feel flustered with her smiles and her own blushing whenever they met.

It seemed so natural to Pierre that everyone liked him, and it would have seemed so strange if anyone hadn't, that he couldn't help believing in the sincerity of those around him. Besides, he was always busy and felt in a constant state of mild, cheerful excitement. He felt like the center of some important movement—that people were always expecting something of him, that if he didn't deliver he would disappoint many people, but if he just did this and that, everything would be fine. And so he did what was asked of him, but that happy outcome always remained somewhere in the future.

More than anyone, Prince Vasili took charge of Pierre's affairs and of Pierre himself during those early days. From the death of Count Bezukhov, he never let go of the young man. He had the manner of someone burdened with business, weary and suffering, who nevertheless wouldn't abandon this helpless youth—after all, the son of his old friend and the owner of such enormous wealth—to the whims of fate and the schemes of villains. During his few days in Moscow after Count Bezukhov's death, he would summon Pierre or visit him, telling him what needed to be done in a tired, confident tone, as if adding each time: 'You know I'm overwhelmed with work and it's purely out of kindness that I bother with you, and you know perfectly well that what I'm proposing is the only sensible option.'

"Well, my dear fellow, tomorrow we're off at last," said Prince Vasili one day, closing his eyes and touching Pierre's elbow, speaking as if they had agreed on this long ago and it couldn't be changed. "We leave tomorrow and I'm giving you a place in my carriage. I'm very glad. All our important business here is settled, and I should have left ages ago. Here's something I received from the chancellor. I asked him on your behalf, and you've been accepted into the diplomatic corps and made a Gentleman of the Bedchamber. A diplomatic career now lies open before you."

Despite the weary confidence with which these words were delivered, Pierre, who had been thinking about his future for a long time, wanted to say something. But Prince Vasili cut him off in that special deep, cooing tone he used in extreme cases when special persuasion was needed—a tone that made interruption impossible.

"But my dear, I did this for my own sake, to satisfy my conscience, and there's nothing to thank me for. No one has ever complained about being loved too much. Besides, you're free—you could drop the whole thing tomorrow. But you'll see everything for yourself when you get to Petersburg. It's time you got away from these terrible memories." Prince Vasili sighed. "Yes, yes, my boy. And my valet can ride in your carriage. Oh, I nearly forgot," he added. "You know, my dear, your father and I had some financial matters between us, so I've collected what was due from the Ryazan estate and I'll keep it. You won't be needing it. We'll sort out the accounts later."
By 'what was due from the Ryazan estate,' Prince Vasili meant several thousand rubles in rent payments from Pierre's peasants, which the prince had pocketed for himself.

In Petersburg, as in Moscow, Pierre found the same atmosphere of warmth and friendliness. He couldn't refuse the position—or rather the rank, since he did nothing—that Prince Vasili had arranged for him. Social obligations, invitations, and engagements were so numerous that here, even more than in Moscow, he felt a sense of bewilderment, bustle, and constant expectation of something good that was always just ahead but never quite arrived.

Many of his former bachelor friends were no longer in Petersburg. The Guards had gone to the front. Dolokhov had been demoted to the ranks. Anatole was somewhere in the provinces with the army. Prince Andrew was abroad. So Pierre had no chance to spend his evenings the way he used to, or to have intimate, heart-to-heart conversations with an older friend he respected. His entire time was consumed by dinners and balls, mostly spent at Prince Vasili's house in the company of the stout princess, his wife, and their beautiful daughter Hélène.
Like everyone else, Anna Pavlovna Scherer showed Pierre the change in attitude that society had adopted toward him.

Before, in Anna Pavlovna's presence, Pierre had always felt that everything he said was out of place, tactless, and awkward—that remarks which seemed clever in his head sounded stupid the moment he spoke them, while Hippolyte's dumbest comments somehow came out witty and clever. Now everything Pierre said was charming. Even if Anna Pavlovna didn't say so directly, he could tell she wanted to and only held back out of respect for his modesty.
In the early winter of 1805-06, Pierre received one of Anna Pavlovna's usual pink invitations, with a note added: 'You will find the beautiful Hélène here, whom it is always a delight to see.'

When he read that line, Pierre felt for the first time that some connection that others could see had formed between him and Hélène. The thought both alarmed him—as if some obligation were being placed on him that he couldn't fulfill—and pleased him as an intriguing possibility.

Anna Pavlovna's party was like the previous one, except this time the novelty she offered her guests was not Mortemart but a diplomat fresh from Berlin, bringing the latest details about Emperor Alexander's visit to Potsdam and how the two great friends had pledged an unbreakable alliance to uphold justice against the enemy of mankind. Anna Pavlovna greeted Pierre with a touch of sadness, clearly referring to the young man's recent loss of his father (everyone felt obligated to remind Pierre how devastated he must be by the death of a father he had barely known), and her sadness matched the grand melancholy she displayed when mentioning Her Most August Majesty the Empress. Pierre felt flattered. Anna Pavlovna arranged the groups in her drawing room with her usual skill. The larger group, which included Prince Vasili and the generals, had the diplomat's attention. Another group gathered around the tea table. Pierre wanted to join the first, but Anna Pavlovna—in the excited state of a battlefield commander with a thousand brilliant ideas and not enough time to execute them all—spotted Pierre, touched his sleeve with her finger, and said:

"Wait, I have something in mind for you this evening." She glanced at Hélène and smiled. "My dear Hélène, be kind to my poor aunt who adores you. Go keep her company for ten minutes. And so it won't be too boring, here is the dear count, who I'm sure won't refuse to go with you."
The beauty went to the aunt, but Anna Pavlovna held Pierre back, looking as if she had some final essential instructions.

"Isn't she magnificent?" she said to Pierre, pointing to the stately beauty gliding away. "And such poise! For such a young woman, such perfect manners! It comes from the heart. The man who wins her will be lucky indeed. With her, even the most ordinary man would have a brilliant position in society. Don't you agree? I just wanted to hear your opinion." And Anna Pavlovna let Pierre go.
Pierre sincerely agreed about Hélène's perfect manners. Whenever he thought of Hélène, it was only of her beauty and her remarkable ability to appear silently dignified in any social setting.

The old aunt received the two young people in her corner but seemed more interested in hiding her adoration for Hélène and showing her fear of Anna Pavlovna. She looked at her niece as if asking what to do with these visitors. As she left them, Anna Pavlovna touched Pierre's sleeve again: "I hope you won't say it's boring at my house again." She glanced at Hélène.

Hélène smiled with a look that said she couldn't imagine anyone seeing her without being enchanted. The aunt coughed, swallowed, and told Hélène in French how pleased she was to see her, then turned to Pierre with the same greeting and the same look. In the middle of a halting, dull conversation, Hélène turned to Pierre with the beautiful, radiant smile she gave everyone. Pierre was so used to that smile, and it meant so little to him, that he paid no attention. The aunt was talking about a collection of snuffboxes that had belonged to Pierre's father, Count Bezukhov, and showed them her own. Princess Hélène asked to see the portrait of the aunt's husband on the lid.
"That's probably by Vinesse," said Pierre, naming a famous miniaturist, and he leaned over the table to take the snuffbox while trying to hear the conversation at the other table.

He half stood up, meaning to walk around, but the aunt handed him the snuffbox across Hélène's back. Hélène leaned forward to make room and looked back with a smile. She was wearing, as always at evening parties, a dress cut very low at the front and back, in the fashion of the time. Her bust, which had always seemed like marble to Pierre, was so close that his nearsighted eyes couldn't help noticing the living warmth of her neck and shoulders, so near his lips that he would only have had to bend his head slightly to touch them. He felt the warmth of her body, smelled her perfume, and heard the creaking of her corset as she moved. He no longer saw her marble beauty as a complete whole unified with her dress—instead, he saw all the charm of her body barely concealed by her clothing. And once he had seen this, he couldn't unsee it, just as you can't restore an illusion you've seen through.

"So you've never noticed before how beautiful I am?" Hélène seemed to say. "You hadn't realized I'm a woman? Yes, I am a woman who could belong to anyone—to you too," said her glance. And at that moment Pierre felt that Hélène not only could but must be his wife, and that it couldn't be any other way.

He knew this as surely as if he had been standing at the altar with her. How and when it would happen he didn't know; he didn't even know if it would be a good thing (he even felt, for some reason he couldn't explain, that it would be a bad thing), but he knew it would happen.

Pierre dropped his eyes, then raised them again, trying to see her once more as a distant beauty far removed from him—the way he had seen her every day until then. But he could no longer do it. He couldn't, just as a man who has mistaken a tuft of steppe grass for a tree through the mist can never see it as a tree again once he recognizes what it is. She was terribly close. She already had power over him. Between them there was no barrier except the barrier of his own will.
"Well, I'll leave you in your little corner," came Anna Pavlovna's voice. "I can see you're doing just fine there."
And Pierre, anxiously trying to remember if he'd done anything wrong, looked around with a blush. It seemed to him that everyone knew what had happened to him, just as he knew it himself.
A little later, when he joined the larger group, Anna Pavlovna said to him: "I hear you're renovating your Petersburg house?"
This was true. The architect had told him it was necessary, and Pierre, without knowing why, was having his enormous Petersburg mansion redone.

"That's a good thing, but don't move out of Prince Vasili's. It's good to have a friend like the prince," she said, smiling at Prince Vasili. "I know a thing or two about that, don't I? And you're still so young. You need advice. Don't be angry with me for exercising an old woman's privilege."

She paused, as women always do after mentioning their age. "If you marry, that will be a different matter," she continued, her glance linking them both. Pierre didn't look at Hélène and she didn't look at him. But she was just as terrifyingly close. He mumbled something and blushed.

When he got home, he couldn't sleep for a long time, thinking about what had happened. What had happened? Nothing. He had simply realized that the woman he had known since childhood—about whom he would say casually when her beauty was mentioned, 'Yes, she's good-looking'—he had realized that this woman could be his.

"But she's stupid. I've said so myself," he thought. "There's something wrong, something ugly, about the feeling she stirs in me. I've been told that her brother Anatole was in love with her and she with him, that there was a real scandal, and that's why he was sent away. Hippolyte is her brother... Prince Vasili is her father... This is wrong..." he reflected. But even as he thought this—and the thought was still incomplete—he caught himself smiling and realized a completely different train of thought had taken over. While thinking about her flaws, he was simultaneously dreaming about how she would be his wife, how she would love him and become entirely different, and how everything he had thought and heard about her might be false. And once again he saw her, not as Prince Vasili's daughter, but her whole body only veiled by its gray dress. "But no! Why didn't this occur to me before?" And again he told himself it was impossible, that there would be something unnatural, something dishonorable about this marriage. He remembered her past words and looks and the words and looks of those who had seen them together. He recalled Anna Pavlovna's comments about his house, remembered a thousand similar hints from Prince Vasili and others, and was seized with terror that he had somehow already bound himself to do something clearly wrong that he ought not to do. But even as he was convincing himself of this, in another part of his mind her image rose in all its feminine beauty.
